title: Water into Wine and the Cleansing of the Temple
summary: At a wedding in Cana, when the wine runs out, Jesus has servants fill six stone purification jars with water, which becomes the best wine of the feast. John calls this the first of his signs, revealing his glory. At Passover in Jerusalem, Jesus drives the animal sellers and money changers out of the temple courts and, when challenged for a sign, speaks of destroying this temple and raising it in three days, meaning his body.
story:
Chapter 1 ended with Jesus promising Nathanael that he would see greater things. Here the first of them happens, on the third day after the calling of Philip and Nathanael. The two scenes of this chapter belong together. In Cana, a village in the Galilean hills, Jesus replaces the water of Jewish purification with abundant wine; in Jerusalem, at the center of Israel's worship, he confronts the temple and speaks of his own body as the true temple. Both show that something new has arrived that fulfills and surpasses Israel's institutions, and both are acts of the Son in what he calls his Father's house and his Father's world.

The chapter also introduces threads that run through the whole Gospel: Jesus' hour, which has not yet come; the signs, which reveal his glory and draw out faith or misunderstanding; and the disciples' remembering, which only after the resurrection grasps what Jesus meant. It ends with a warning that belief based on signs alone can be thin, which prepares for Nicodemus, a man who comes to Jesus because of the signs, in chapter 3.
historical:
Cana is mentioned only in John (2:1, 4:46, 21:2), where it is Nathanael's hometown. Josephus, who commanded Jewish forces in Galilee at the start of the revolt against Rome in AD 66, says that he stayed for a time at a Galilean village called Cana (Life 86). Two sites claim it. The traditional pilgrim site is Kafr Kanna, a few miles northeast of Nazareth on the road to Tiberias, where churches mark the wedding today. Many archaeologists favor Khirbet Qana, about eight miles north of Nazareth above the Beit Netofa valley, excavated from 1998 under Douglas Edwards and later Tom McCollough. It was a Jewish village in the Roman period, and a cave complex there was venerated by Christian pilgrims from the Byzantine to the Crusader periods, with a shelf apparently made for stone jars. Capernaum, where Jesus goes next (verse 12), was a fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee.

Stone jars like those in verse 6 are one of the most common finds in first-century Jewish Galilee and Judea. They were carved from soft chalk limestone, and workshops have been excavated, among them one at Reina near Nazareth. Their popularity rests on a purity rule later written into the Mishnah: vessels of stone, like those of dung or earth, do not contract ritual impurity (m. Kelim 10:1), so they could keep water clean for the washing of hands and vessels (Mark 7:3-4). Each jar held two or three metrētai, a Greek liquid measure of about 39 liters or ten gallons, so the six held some 120 to 180 gallons.

The temple Jesus entered was Herod the Great's rebuilding of the second temple. Josephus says Herod began it in the eighteenth year of his reign, about 20 or 19 BC (Antiquities 15.380; Jewish War 1.401 gives the fifteenth year), that the sanctuary itself was finished in a year and a half (Antiquities 15.421), and that work on the whole complex was still going on under the Roman governor Albinus in AD 62 to 64 (Antiquities 20.219), only a few years before the Romans destroyed it in AD 70. Forty-six years from 20/19 BC points to the Passover of about AD 27 or 28, a clue many use to date the start of Jesus' ministry. Because the Greek verb in verse 20 can mean ‘this sanctuary has stood built for forty-six years’, some scholars count from the sanctuary's completion instead and arrive at a slightly later date; the difference is a year or two.

The trade itself was legal and useful. Every Jewish man paid an annual half-shekel to the temple (Exodus 30:13), and the Mishnah says money changers set up tables in the provinces on the fifteenth of Adar and in the temple itself on the twenty-fifth, about three weeks before Passover (m. Shekalim 1:3). The tax had to be paid in the high-silver coinage of Tyre (t. Ketubbot 13:20). Doves were the offering of the poor (Leviticus 12:8), and the Mishnah remembers a time when a pair cost a gold denarius until Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel changed a ruling so that the price fell (m. Keritot 1:7). The selling most likely took place in the vast outer court, open to Gentiles, and in or near the Royal Stoa that Herod built along its southern edge (Antiquities 15.411-416).
cultural:
A village wedding was the largest celebration most families ever held. The bride was brought in procession to the groom's home, and the feast could last up to a week (Judges 14:12 speaks of the seven days of Samson's feast). The groom's family provided food and wine, and neighbors often contributed, so a shortage was not only a practical failure but a public shame in a culture where honor and hospitality mattered greatly. Wine was the ordinary drink of celebration and a sign of God's blessing, “wine that gladdens the heart of man” (Psalm 104:15). Greeks and Jews alike usually mixed it with water at table, and Scripture condemns drunkenness while never treating wine itself as evil. The master of the banquet (architriklinos) oversaw the tables and tasted the wine; Sirach 32:1-2 gives advice to a man chosen to preside at a feast. His remark in verse 10 describes the custom of serving the best wine while palates are fresh; the verb (methuō) means to drink freely or become drunk, and he is describing hosts in general, not reporting that this party had become a drunken one.

Jesus' address to his mother as Woman (gunai) sounds cold in English but was a courteous form of address; he uses it for the Samaritan woman (4:21), for Mary Magdalene (20:15), and for his mother again at the cross (19:26). What does mark distance is the phrase that follows, literally ‘what to me and to you?’, a Hebrew idiom (mah li walak) found in the Old Testament (Judges 11:12, 2 Samuel 16:10, 1 Kings 17:18) and in the Gospels on the lips of demons (Mark 1:24). It sets aside a request, sometimes sharply and sometimes gently. Jesus' actions are governed by his hour, not by family request, and Mary's response (verse 5) shows she took it as neither a rebuke nor a refusal.

The brothers of Jesus (verse 12) are named in Mark 6:3 as James, Joses, Judas, and Simon. Christians have understood them in three ways since the fourth century: as younger children of Joseph and Mary (the view Helvidius argued and many Protestants hold today), as children of Joseph by an earlier marriage (the view of Epiphanius and of Orthodox tradition), or as cousins (Jerome, Against Helvidius, around 383, followed in much Western Catholic teaching). The text itself does not settle the question. At the temple, the whip of cords (phragellion, from the Latin flagellum) was made on the spot from rope or rushes, and Jesus uses it to drive out the sheep and cattle; John does not say he struck anyone. The Jews in verses 18 and 20 are, as often in John, the temple authorities, and the question they ask, what sign proves his authority, was a fair one to put to anyone acting as a prophet in the temple.
literary:
John tells the Cana story with great economy, and much is left unsaid: we never learn whose wedding it was, how the water became wine, or what the guests thought, only that the servants knew. The story turns on a pattern that recurs in John: a request, an apparent refusal, a persistent faith, and then an action that exceeds the request (compare the royal official in 4:46-54 and Martha and Mary in chapter 11). Its key sentence is its conclusion in verse 11, which calls the act the beginning of his signs (archēn tōn sēmeiōn), says it revealed his glory, and says his disciples believed. The second sign is also done at Cana and is numbered (4:54), so chapters 2 to 4 are framed as a section running from Cana to Cana, a structure noticed by source critics such as Robert Fortna (The Gospel of Signs, 1970), who thought John drew on a numbered collection of miracle stories, and by narrative readers who see it as John's own design.

The temple scene follows John's characteristic pattern of misunderstanding. Jesus speaks of a temple; his hearers think of the building; the narrator explains that he meant his body (verse 21). The disciples understand only later, and John openly tells the reader that their memory and faith were shaped by what came after (verse 22), a remark repeated at 12:16 and grounded in the promise that the Spirit will remind them of everything Jesus said (14:26). The two scenes also mirror each other: a family feast and a national feast, water for purification and a temple for sacrifice, a quiet sign that only servants see and a public act that everyone sees.

The closing verses (23 to 25) turn on wordplay. Many believed (episteusan) in his name, but Jesus did not entrust (episteuen) himself to them, the same verb used twice. He did not need anyone's testimony about man (anthrōpos), for he knew what was in a man. The next verse, 3:1, introduces “a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus”, the first example of what Jesus knows.

outline.t: A wedding at Cana; the wine runs out
The first sign reveals his glory
Destroy this temple: the sign of his body
Faith based on signs; Jesus knows the heart

doctrines.note: Verse 11 says Jesus “revealed His glory” at Cana. The glory that filled the tabernacle and was seen in the Word made flesh (1:14) is shown here not in fire or cloud but in a gift of joy at a village wedding, and it will be shown most fully when the hour comes and the Son is glorified on the cross (12:23, 17:1).

Jesus acts in the temple as a son in his Father's house, then speaks of “the temple of His body” (verse 21). The place where God meets his people is moving from a building to a person, a theme John develops when Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that true worship will belong to neither Gerizim nor Jerusalem (4:21-23).

“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again” (verse 19) is Jesus' first prediction of his resurrection in John, and it presents him as the agent of his own raising, as in 10:18. The disciples' belief after Easter rests on two things together: the Scripture and the word Jesus had spoken (verse 22).

The prophets pictured the age of salvation as a time of abundant wine (Amos 9:13, Joel 3:18, Isaiah 25:6), and Genesis 49:11 describes the ruler from Judah washing his garments in wine. By providing some 120 to 180 gallons of the best wine, Jesus signals that the age of promise has arrived.

The chapter shows two kinds of believing. The disciples believe at Cana (verse 11) and believe more deeply after the resurrection (verse 22). Many in Jerusalem believe because of signs, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them (verses 23 to 25). Faith that begins with signs is not rejected, but it must grow into trust in Jesus himself.

words.note: Sēmeion, sign. It occurs about 77 times in the New Testament and 17 times in John, which uses it as its main word for Jesus' miracles. The Synoptic Gospels more often call them dynameis, mighty works, a word John never uses for them. BDAG defines a sign as a distinguishing mark or event by which something is known, and in John the signs point beyond themselves to who Jesus is. Signs can lead to faith (verse 11) but can also produce a thin belief that Jesus does not trust (verses 23 to 25), and in 20:30-31 the written record of signs becomes the means by which later readers believe.

Hōra, hour. It occurs 26 times in John. It can mean simply a time of day (1:39, 4:6), but in Jesus' phrase my hour it means the appointed time of his death, resurrection, and return to the Father. Through the first half of the Gospel it has not yet come (2:4, 7:30, 8:20); at 12:23 Jesus announces that it has, and 13:1 and 17:1 repeat it. Even at a wedding his actions are ordered toward that hour.

Doxa, glory. It occurs about 166 times in the New Testament and 19 times in John. In ordinary Greek it meant opinion or reputation, but the Greek Old Testament used it to translate the Hebrew kavod, the weighty, radiant presence of God (Exodus 40:34). John uses it in that biblical sense: Jesus' glory is the Father's glory made visible, seen at Cana, at Lazarus's tomb (11:40), and supremely in the lifting up of the Son on the cross.

Katharismos, cleansing, purification. It occurs seven times in the New Testament and twice in John (2:6, 3:25). Here it names the ritual washings for which the stone jars stood ready, practices of care for holiness, not empty formalism. The sign turns the water kept for purification into wine for celebration, suggesting that what the rites prepared for has now arrived, much as 1:17 contrasts the law given through Moses with grace and truth come through Jesus Christ.

Naos, sanctuary. John distinguishes two words. Hieron (verses 14 and 15) is the whole temple complex, with its courts where the traders were; naos (verses 19, 20, and 21, its only uses in John) is the sanctuary, the house of God proper. Jesus uses naos for his body: he is the true dwelling of God, as the Word who tabernacled among us (1:14). The distinction is common in Greek usage, though not every writer keeps it strictly.

Zēlos, zeal, ardor, and in a negative sense jealousy. It occurs 16 times in the New Testament. In verse 17 it comes from Psalm 69:9, where a righteous sufferer says that zeal for God's house has consumed him and that the insults aimed at God have fallen on him. Psalm 69 is among the psalms most quoted in the New Testament, and John returns to it (15:25; compare 19:28-29 with Psalm 69:21). Zeal here is love for God's honor that costs the one who has it.

Pisteuō, to believe, trust, entrust. It occurs about 241 times in the New Testament and 98 times in John, while the noun faith (pistis) never appears in John at all. John prefers the verb because believing is something one does: coming to Jesus, receiving him, continuing in his word. In verses 23 and 24 John plays on the verb's range: people believed in his name, but Jesus did not entrust himself to them.

christ:
Both scenes reveal Jesus as the one in whom Israel's hopes are fulfilled. At Cana he provides the wine of the promised age. The prophets had spoken of mountains dripping with sweet wine (Amos 9:13, Joel 3:18) and of a feast of aged wine on God's mountain (Isaiah 25:6), and a Jewish apocalypse from around AD 100, 2 Baruch 29:5, pictures the Messiah's age with vines of fantastic yield. Scripture also pictures God as a bridegroom and his people as a bride (Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2:19). In the next chapter the Baptist calls Jesus the bridegroom (3:29), and the Bible's story ends with “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). The link between Cana and these texts is thematic rather than a direct fulfillment of one prophecy, but John clearly means the reader to hear it: the bridegroom has come, and the good wine has been kept until now. He does it by transforming water set apart for purification, a sign that he brings what the old rites pointed toward.

The word hour and the address Woman tie Cana to the cross. When the hour has come, Jesus again speaks to his mother as Woman and gives her to the beloved disciple (19:26-27), and on the cross he says “I am thirsty” and is given sour wine (19:28-29). The joy of Cana is paid for at Golgotha.

In the temple Jesus acts with the authority of the Son in his Father's house, fulfilling Malachi 3:1, where the Lord “will suddenly come to His temple” to refine its worship, and Zechariah 14:21, where in the day of the Lord there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the Lord (the Hebrew word can also mean trader, and many versions render it so). His disciples remember Psalm 69:9, the lament of a righteous sufferer, and the verb consume hints at where Jesus' zeal will lead him. His answer to the demand for a sign points to the greatest sign, his resurrection. The other Gospels record the charge at his trial that he had said he would destroy the temple and build another in three days (Mark 14:58), and the mockery at the cross (Mark 15:29); John explains what he meant. He is the new temple, the place where God meets his people, and after his body is destroyed and raised, worship will center on him rather than on a building in Jerusalem.
interpretation:
The church read Cana from early on as a revelation of Christ's glory and a blessing on creation and marriage. In the West the feast of the Epiphany joined three manifestations, the Magi, the baptism in the Jordan, and the wedding at Cana, and an ancient antiphon for Epiphany morning prayer weaves the three together, calling Cana a royal wedding. The historic Western lectionary read John 2:1-11 on the second Sunday after Epiphany, which is where Luther's Church Postil and the Book of Common Prayer place it, and the Revised Common Lectionary keeps it there in Year C. The 1662 Prayer Book's marriage service opens by saying that Christ adorned and beautified marriage with his presence and first miracle at Cana.

The fathers disagreed about Mary's part. John Chrysostom (Homily 21 on John, around 390) thought she wished to gain credit through her son and that Jesus corrected her. Augustine (Tractates on John 8 and 9) read the six jars as the six ages of history, from Adam to Christ, full of prophecy that becomes wine when Christ is understood in it. Medieval and later Catholic devotion saw Mary at Cana as an intercessor who directs others to her Son; John Paul II's encyclical Redemptoris Mater (1987, section 21) describes Cana as Mary's motherly mediation, and his letter Rosarium Virginis Mariae (2002) made the wedding the second of the Luminous Mysteries of the Rosary. Protestant readers have often stressed instead the distance Jesus puts between his hour and his mother's request. Both traditions draw on her words in verse 5, which Catholic and Protestant preachers alike treat as the heart of the scene.

The temple scene raised the question of order early. Origen (Commentary on John, book 10) judged that the Gospels cannot be harmonized here and argued that the spiritual truth is sometimes preserved in what is historically inexact. Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels 2.67) and later Calvin in his commentary held that Jesus cleared the temple twice. Modern critical scholarship has mostly assumed one event. E. P. Sanders (Jesus and Judaism, 1985) argued that it was not a cleansing of abuses but a symbolic act announcing the temple's destruction and renewal, and Paula Fredriksen has questioned whether the scene happened as told at all. Rudolf Bultmann (1941) and Robert Fortna (1970) traced the Cana story to a source of miracle stories, and Bultmann saw in it an echo of Dionysus; Martin Hengel (in The Glory of Christ in the New Testament, 1987) answered that its roots lie in the Old Testament and Jewish hope, while John's Greek readers would also have heard it as a contrast with the wine god. Jewish scholars, among them Adele Reinhartz in The Jewish Annotated New Testament (2011) and Cast Out of the Covenant (2018), have pressed Christian readers to notice how the Jews in verses 18 to 20 have been heard, and misheard, through the centuries.

In art, Giotto painted both scenes in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua (about 1305), and Paolo Veronese's Wedding at Cana (1562 to 1563), painted for the refectory of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice and taken to Paris by Napoleon's army in 1797, is the largest painting in the Louvre. El Greco painted the temple scene at least four times, beginning around 1570, and in Counter-Reformation Spain it was read as a picture of the church purged of heresy. The Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 13 to 22 on the third Sunday in Lent in Year B.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from translation rather than manuscripts. In verse 4, older versions render the idiom literally, ‘Woman, what have I to do with thee?’ (KJV), which sounds harsher than the Greek; modern versions paraphrase, ‘Woman, why does this concern us?’ (BSB) or ‘what does this have to do with me?’ (ESV). In verse 6 the King James Version's ‘two or three firkins apiece’ uses an old English measure for the Greek metrētēs; modern versions convert to gallons or liters. In verse 10 the KJV's ‘when men have well drunk’ and the BSB's ‘after the guests are drunk’ render the same verb, which can mean either.

There are also manuscript differences. In verse 3 the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and some Old Latin manuscripts read a longer sentence, that they had no wine because the wine of the wedding had been used up, and then Jesus' mother spoke; most manuscripts and all modern versions have the shorter text. In verse 17 the best manuscripts have the future tense, ‘will consume Me’, where the standard text of the Greek Psalm (Psalm 68:10 in its numbering) has the past, ‘has consumed me’. Later manuscripts assimilated John to the Psalm, and so the King James Version reads ‘hath eaten me up’. The future is almost certainly original and appears to be John's own adjustment, pointing ahead to the cross. Minor variants in verses 12 and 15 (his disciples or the disciples, and whether the coins are singular or plural) do not affect the sense.

teach.big: Jesus reveals his glory by bringing the joy that Israel's rites anticipated and by claiming that his own body, destroyed and raised, is the true meeting place of God and his people.

outline.t: Jesus' first sign begins with an ordinary family crisis, and Mary's words, ‘Do whatever He tells you’, model trust that leaves the timing to him.
Water kept for purification becomes more and better wine than anyone needed: the new age brings abundance, not merely repair.
A sign is meant to reveal glory and awaken faith, and here it does so for the disciples.
The Son acts with zeal for his Father's house, and that zeal will cost him his life.
The sign Jesus offers is his death and resurrection, and true understanding comes by remembering his word in the light of Easter.
Jesus knows every heart and does not entrust himself to interest that goes no deeper than miracles.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first turns Cana into a debate about alcohol. Some nineteenth-century temperance writers argued that the wine was unfermented grape juice, but the word oinos and the master's remark about drunkenness show that it was wine; on the other side, the story does not license drunkenness, which Scripture condemns. The point is the arrival of messianic joy, not a rule about drink. The second makes Mary either a meddler whom Jesus rebukes or a figure whose request governs his action. The text holds both his independence (my hour) and her trust (verse 5), and teachers should let the tension stand while noting honestly that Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions weigh it differently.

With the temple scene, avoid using verse 15 to justify anger or violence in general; Jesus' act is a prophetic sign by the Son in his Father's house, and John does not say he struck anyone. Avoid reducing it to a lesson about church fundraising, which trivializes the claim that his body replaces the temple. Avoid treating the Jews of verses 18 to 20 as a picture of Jewish people generally; they are temple authorities asking a fair question. And avoid making verses 23 to 25 a verdict that anyone whose faith began with a miracle is false: the disciples' own faith began with a sign in verse 11.
teach.pastoral: The Cana story will press on people in the room for whom alcohol has meant addiction, loss, or abuse. Teach it without mocking abstinence and without glamorizing drinking, and remember that the story's joy is in Jesus' presence and gift, not in the wine as such. It may also touch people who have known the shame of a family event that went wrong, or of poverty exposed in public; Jesus' quiet provision, known only to the servants, honors the family without exposing them. Those who have been hurt by religious institutions that treated worship as a business may find the temple scene a relief, and they need to hear that Jesus' answer to a corrupted temple was not cynicism but himself.

hard.q: Did Jesus clear the temple at the beginning of his ministry, as John says, or at the end, as the other Gospels say?
hard.a:
The objection is simple and strong. Matthew, Mark, and Luke place the temple incident in Jesus' last week, where it leads directly to the plot against him (Mark 11:15-18), while John places it at his first Passover, two or three years earlier. Critics since the nineteenth century have taken this as a clear contradiction, and many historians agree with E. P. Sanders (Jesus and Judaism, 1985) that an act like this in the temple at Passover best explains why the authorities moved against Jesus when they did, which favors the Synoptic setting. Paula Fredriksen has gone further and doubted that the scene happened as the Gospels describe it.

There are three main responses. The first, held by Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels 2.67), Calvin, and many modern conservative commentators, is that there were two cleansings. John has Jesus in Jerusalem at several Passovers, the wording differs (a marketplace in John, a den of robbers in the Synoptics), and a repeated prophetic protest is plausible. The second, held by most critical scholars, is that there was one event, placed at the end by the Synoptic Gospels because their outline has only one visit to Jerusalem, and placed at the start by John as a programmatic statement of what Jesus' whole mission means, much as Luke opens Jesus' ministry with the Nazareth sermon (Luke 4:16-30). Ancient biographers often arranged material by theme rather than strict sequence, and on this view John's order is theological rather than chronological. The third, a minority, holds that John's early date is the historical one, noting that the forty-six years of verse 20 fit the late 20s AD and that John elsewhere shows detailed knowledge of Jerusalem. Christians who hold a high view of Scripture's truthfulness are found on both sides of the one-or-two question, as Origen and Augustine already were, and the point of the event, Jesus' authority over the temple and his body as its fulfillment, is the same in all four Gospels.

hard.q: Did Jesus really turn water into wine, or is this a legend modeled on the wine god Dionysus?
hard.a:
The skeptical case has two parts. The first is general: David Hume (An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, 1748, section 10) argued that no testimony can make a miracle more probable than the uniform experience against it, and David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) treated the Cana story as a myth that grew from Old Testament and messianic imagery. The second is specific: Rudolf Bultmann (1941) and others pointed to stories of Dionysus, the Greek god of wine, who was said to change water into wine at his festivals. Pausanias, writing in the second century AD, reports that at Elis priests set three empty basins in a sealed building during the festival called Thyia and found them full of wine the next morning (Description of Greece 6.26.1-2). On this view John has presented Jesus as a better Dionysus for Greek readers.

Responses begin with the differences. The Dionysus stories are cult legends tied to temples and festivals; the Cana story is set in a Jewish village, uses Jewish purity jars, draws no attention to itself, and is known only to servants. Martin Hengel (1987) argued that its background is chiefly the Old Testament and Jewish hope for the wine of the messianic age (Amos 9:13, Isaiah 25:6), though he allowed that John's Greek readers would also hear a contrast with Dionysus. Others note that Cana is otherwise obscure, which is odd for an invented setting. On the general question, whether miracles can happen depends on prior beliefs about God and nature; C. S. Lewis (Miracles, 1947) argued that Hume's case assumes what it sets out to prove, and Craig Keener (Miracles, 2011) has documented how widespread eyewitness claims of extraordinary events are. The church confesses that the one through whom all things were made (1:3) can act in his creation. Historians who do not share that confession will judge the report differently, and a reader should know that the dispute turns as much on worldview as on evidence.

observe: What does Mary say to Jesus, what does he answer, and what does she then tell the servants?
Who knew where the good wine came from, and who did not?
What reason does verse 17 give for the disciples' remembering, and what does verse 22 say they remembered after the resurrection?
interpret: Why do you think John chose water jars for purification as the setting for the first sign? What might the change from water to wine signify?
What does Jesus mean by calling his body a temple, and how does that change where people meet God?
Many believed in Jesus' name because of the signs, yet he did not entrust himself to them. What is missing in their believing?
apply: Mary told the servants, ‘Do whatever He tells you.’ What is Jesus telling you to do that you have been reluctant to act on?
Jesus' zeal for his Father's house cost him. What in your own worship or church life has become more about transaction than about God?
Is your trust in Jesus resting on what he can do for you, or on who he is? What would it look like for it to grow deeper?
